In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
The White Tiger’s animal perspective is an attempt to subvert humanist narratives of the tiger economy, and that this attempt is both limited by and productive of the novel’s humanism.
the novel’s narrative strategy of animalization, which is premised on a humanist perspective, is undermined by the becoming-animal of its central character.
The White Tiger, through its use of animal metaphors, is a postcolonial critique of the Indian tiger economy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have argued that The White Tiger is a posthuman novel, which, in the context of the postcolonial, has the potential to be a radical text.
the novel’s representation of the animal is a means of representing the subaltern, but it is a means that ultimately fails to represent the subaltern as an ethical subject.
the tiger in The White Tiger functions as a symbol of the animalized subaltern, who is not a human, but is humanized.
The main takeaway from our work is that

Adiga’s novel, in the end, offers a critique of the humanist narrative of the tiger economy that is not premised on the animal’s abjection but rather on the animal’s exposure to the human and vice versa, and the potential of this exposure for the production of a new ethical subjectivity.
the novel, in the way that it uses animal tropes, is not a straightforwardly posthuman text, but it does offer a critique of the humanist assumptions of the neoliberal tiger economy.

the animalization of the Indian subaltern is a key component of the tiger economy, and that the tiger economy itself is an anthropocentric fiction that relies on a devaluation of animal life in order to maintain its own hegemony.
